title: Lights Out? Wargaming a Chinese Blockade of Taiwan
summary: CSIS wargame study of a Chinese blockade of Taiwan: costly for all sides, energy is Taiwan's weak point, escalation pressures at every level, US help essential.

assertions.quote: blockade is not a lowcost, low-risk operation for China. There's the possibility of escalation and also alienating the global community.

verdicts.note: Wargames (CSIS and others) consistently find blockades bring casualties and escalation risk for China, though these are models, not observed outcomes.

assertions.quote: The second is that there are escalatory pressures at every level.

verdicts.note: US commitments under the Taiwan Relations Act and wargame results make escalation plausible, though its probability is uncertain.

assertions.quote: Taiwan cannot face China alone. The disparity in economic and military power is too great.

verdicts.note: China's defence budget and forces dwarf Taiwan's, and wargames find Taiwan's survival depends on US intervention.

CSIS lists US entry into the war within days, with its full range of capabilities, as a necessary condition for defeating an invasion, alongside Taiwan resisting, US use of Japanese bases and enough anti-ship missiles.

assertions.quote: Energy emerges ships are the critical factors for resilience because Taiwan does not produce very much energy on its own.

verdicts.note: Taiwan imports almost all of its energy and holds only days to weeks of LNG in reserve.

assertions.quote: how much the preparations that Taiwan could feasibly do could uh improve their situation.

verdicts.note: Modelling shows larger fuel inventories and hardened power extend Taiwan's endurance, though this is untested in practice.

assertions.quote: None of them were adequate to keep uh the island supplied.

verdicts.note: Taiwan's population and bulk energy needs far exceed what Berlin's 1948 airlift carried; aircraft cannot move fuel at that scale.

assertions.quote: 27 being a year that Xiinping had laid out for the PLA to say be ready by this time

verdicts.note: DoD 2025: the PLA's 2027 goals require it to be able to achieve 'strategic decisive victory' over Taiwan, and it keeps refining invasion, firepower-strike and blockade options to force unification, testing their components in 2024 exercises.
Davidson cites the numbers of ships, aircraft and rockets China has fielded and its advancing capabilities, and calls seizing Taiwan one of its ambitions before 2050.
DDIS: Xi set 2027 as the deadline for the military to be ready to invade Taiwan, likely to be met, and the build-up is meant to let China prevail in a war over Taiwan.
US intelligence says the PLA keeps developing plans and capabilities to take Taiwan by force if directed and is making steady but uneven progress.

assertions.quote: It's so easy to escalate. It's so hard to deescalate.

verdicts.note: Many wars ran longer than planned, but many crises and limited clashes were de-escalated too.

CSIS cites Nolan: translating combat into a political result the other side accepts is 'the single hardest thing to do', and expects a Taiwan war could drag on episodically; this is argument, not data.
RAND concludes the Ukraine war shows that finely calibrating and managing escalation 'is nearly impossible', which supports the claim for wars with nuclear powers without measuring start versus stop.
Braumoeller: catastrophic wars result from decisions by people who don't want to stop fighting, and a war's chance of growing very large has not changed.

assertions.quote: the costs of defending Taiwan in my view would be higher than the benefits

verdicts.note: A judgment about the value of US interests that evidence cannot settle.
CSIS documents the costs of defending Taiwan but explicitly 'does not take a position on whether the benefits of defending Taiwan outweigh the prospective costs'.
